(1) the A V approach is effective in improving the spoken language outcomes of children who are born deaf or with hearing loss, and (2) the A V model is cost effective in terms of the resources required.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the Auditory-Verbal approach, and the outcomes of children with hearing impairment and their families who receive this intervention.
the evaluation of the Auditory-Verbal approach to the habilitation of children with hearing loss and the development of the Auditory Skills Checklist as an outcome measure for the approach.
the development of a new approach to the study of the effects of the A V intervention on the effectiveness of A V intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive evidence to support the use of A V intervention for children who have hearing impairment.

the evidence base for A V is limited, that there is no clear evidence that A V is more effective than other approaches, that there is evidence that the A V approach can be effective, and that there is a need for more rigorous and comprehensive research.
the evidence base is insufficient to support or refute the efficacy of A V intervention, and that the approach is not justified on this basis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence base for AV is not as strong as it might appear.
the evidence base for A V is not strong enough to justify the approach as the only intervention model.
the evidence is not sufficient to support a claim of efficacy of A V for all children with hearing loss.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evidence for AV is not strong, and that the evidence is not strong in part because there are no large, high quality studies.
